text: Icie Gertrude Macy Hoobler (July 23, 1892 – January 6, 1984) was an American biochemist known for her research in human nutrition, particularly focusing on mothers and children. Despite facing gender-based discrimination, she became the first woman chair of a local section of the American Chemical Society and earned 22 awards and honors for her laboratory's research. She grew up on a farm in Gallatin, Missouri, where her interest in science developed from observing animal maturation and exploring her family's property. A childhood trip to the mountains of Arkansas, where she saw sick children in poor living conditions, sparked her compassion for children's wellness. Before pursuing chemistry, she spent three years at Central Female College in Lexington, Missouri, against her own wishes, where she met biology teacher Lily Egbert, who encouraged her to pursue science. She then attended the University of Chicago to major in chemistry with a minor in physics, and her advisor sent her to the University of Colorado at Boulder to teach inorganic chemistry. There, she earned her master's degree in 1918; her first project developed a more sensitive cyanide test for autopsies, leading to her first publication, and her second improved an extraction method for tungstic acid from tungsten ores. She also served as a teaching assistant in the physiological chemistry course at the medical school. After completing her master's, she entered a Ph.D. program at Yale University, where she studied physiological chemistry. At the time, Yale admitted only a few female graduate students, and female students faced housing discrimination, as landlords viewed them as "bothersome." Hoobler joined the Graduate Women's Club, which successfully advocated for on-campus housing for female students. During a lecture on the dairy and milk industry, a professor encouraged women to enter human nutrition research, which inspired Hoobler to prioritize the health of mothers, infants, and children. After receiving her Ph.D., she began working at Western Pennsylvania Hospital in Pittsburgh as an assistant chemist, where she encountered severe gender discrimination—she was denied access to men's restrooms and had to use a public restroom half a block away, which led to her developing acute nephritis (kidney inflammation). She was advised to take a year's leave of absence due to this condition. She was also barred from eating in the doctors' dining hall and could not eat in the nurses' dining hall for bureaucratic reasons, so she ate with hospital employees. When she expressed her dissatisfaction to the chief of the laboratory, he told her she would soon get used to the conditions; after two weeks with no improvement, she resigned. The day after her resignation, the hospital's board president questioned the chief of the laboratory about excluding her from the annual staff banquet, leading to improved treatment for Hoobler. Throughout her career, she faced further discrimination, such as when the Chicago Club invited her to speak, not realizing "Icie" was a female name, and she was initially denied entry until her husband negotiated with the board and a re-vote was held. In 1923, during her year of rest from nephritis, she began teaching at the University of California, Berkeley, where she taught a course on food chemistry. She was later offered the position of director of the Nutrition Research Project at the Merril-Palmer School for Motherhood and Child Development, a role she held for 31 years and served as a research consultant from 1954 to 1974. Under her leadership, the laboratory published 300 journal articles and several books on topics including the metabolism of women during the reproductive cycle and the chemistry of the red blood cell. In 1931, Hoobler became the first woman chair of the local section of the American Chemical Society. She received numerous awards, including the Norlin Award from the University of Colorado Boulder, the Garvan–Olin Medal from the American Chemical Society, the Borden Award from the American Home Economics Association, the Osborne Award, and the Mendel Award from the American Institute of Nutrition. She was inducted into the Michigan Women's Hall of Fame in 1984. At age 46, Hoobler married Dr. Raymond Hoobler, who died in 1943 after five years of marriage. In 1982, she returned to her birthplace in Missouri and died two years later in 1984.
